entries.6927f4acd9de0d50ba8540b61719976b5b2f08e3: <div sID="gen31542" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="2Cor.8" sID="2Cor.8"/> <div eID="gen31542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31543" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31544" type="x-p"/> In this and the following chapter Paul is exhorting and directing the Corinthians about a particular work of charity—to relieve the necessities of the poor saints at Jerusalem and in Judea, according to the good example of the churches in Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.26">Rom. xv. 26</reference>. The Christians at Jerusalem, through war, famine, and persecution, had become poor, many of them had fallen into decay, and perhaps most of them were but poor when they first embraced Christianity; for Christ said, "The poor receive the gospel." Now Paul, though he was the apostle of the Gentiles, had a fonder regard, and kind concern, for those among the Jews who were converted to the Christian faith; and, though many of them had not so much affection to the Gentile converts as they ought to have had, yet the apostle would have the Gentiles to be kind to them, and stirred them up to contribute liberally for their relief. Upon this subject he is very copious, and writes very affectingly. In this eighth chapter he acquaints the Corinthians with, and commends, the good example of the Macedonians in this work of charity, and that Titus was sent to Corinth to collect their bounty, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1-2Cor.8.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. He the proceeds to urge this duty with several cogent arguments (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.7-2Cor.8.15">ver. 7-15</reference>), and commends the persons who were employed in this affair, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16-2Cor.8.24">ver. 16-24</reference>.
entries.d9dcfa4e5ec9eb3032d6bf9336e64719f66ebba5: <div eID="gen31544" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31543" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Charity of the Macedonians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia; <hi type="super">2</hi> How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality. 3 For to <hi type="italic">their</hi> power, I bear record, yea, and beyond <hi type="italic">their</hi> power <hi type="italic">they were</hi> willing of themselves; <hi type="super">4</hi> Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and <hi type="italic">take upon us</hi> the fellowship of the ministering to the saints. <hi type="super">5</hi> And <hi type="italic">this they did,</hi> not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God. <hi type="super">6</hi> Insomuch that we desired Titus, that as he had begun, so he would also finish in you the same grace also. <div eID="gen31545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31546" type="x-p"/> Observe here, <div eID="gen31546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31547" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle takes occasion from the good example of the churches of Macedonia, that is, of Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and others in the region of Macedonia, to exhort the Corinthians and the Christians in Achaia to the good work of charity. And, <div eID="gen31547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31548" type="x-p"/> 1. He acquaints them with their great liberality, which he calls <hi type="italic">the grace of God bestowed on the churches,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">v. 1</reference>. Some think the words should be rendered, <hi type="italic">the gift of God given in or by the churches.</hi> He certainly means the charitable gifts of these churches, which are called the grace or gifts of God, either because they were very large, or rather because their charity to the poor saints did proceed from God as the author, and was accompanied with true love to God, which also was manifested this way. The grace of God must be owned as the root and fountain of all the good that is in us, or done by us, at any time; and it is great grace and favour from God, and bestowed on us, if we are made useful to others, and are forward to any good work. <div eID="gen31548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31549" type="x-p"/> 2. He commends the charity of the Macedonians, and sets it forth with good advantage. He tells them, (1.) They were but in a low condition, and themselves in distress, yet they contributed to the relief of others. <hi type="italic">They were in great tribulation and deep poverty,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">v. 2</reference>. It was a time of great affliction with them, as may be seen, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.17">Acts xviii. 17</reference>. The Christians in these parts met with ill treatment, which had reduced them to deep poverty; yet, as they had abundance of joy in the midst of tribulation, they abounded in their liberality; they gave out of a little, trusting in God to provide for them, and make it up to them. (2.) They gave very largely, with <hi type="italic">the riches of liberality</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">v. 2</reference>), that is, as liberally as if they had been rich. It was a large contribution they made, all things considered; it was <hi type="italic">according to,</hi> yea <hi type="italic">beyond, their power</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.3">v. 3</reference>), as much as could well be expected from them, if not more. Note, Though men may condemn the indiscretion, yet God will accept the pious zeal, of those who in real works of piety and charity do rather beyond their power. (3.) They were very ready and forward to this good work. <hi type="italic">They were willing of themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.3">v. 3</reference>), and were so far from needing that Paul should urge and press them with many arguments that they <hi type="italic">prayed him with much entreaty to receive the gift,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.4">v. 4</reference>. It seems Paul was backward to undertake this trust, for <hi type="italic">he would give himself to the word and prayer;</hi> or, it may be, he was apprehensive how ready his enemies would be to reproach and blacken him upon all occasions, and might take a handle against him upon account of so large a sum deposited in his hands, to suspect or accuse him of indiscretion and partiality in the distribution, if not of some injustice. Note, How cautious ministers should be, especially in money-matters, not to give occasion to those who seek occasion to speak reproachfully! (4.) Their charity was founded in true piety, and this was the great commendation of it. They performed this good work in a right method: <hi type="italic">First they gave themselves to the Lord, and then</hi> they gave unto us their contributions, <hi type="italic">by the will of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.5">v. 5</reference>), that is, according as it was the will of God they should do, or to be disposed of as the will of God should be, and for his glory. This, it seems, exceeded the expectation of the apostle; it was more than he hoped for, to see such warm and pious affections shining in these Macedonians, and this good work performed with so much devotion and solemnity. They solemnly, jointly, and unanimously, made a fresh surrender of themselves, and all they had, unto the Lord Jesus Christ. They had done this before, and now they do it again upon this occasion; sanctifying their contributions to God's honour, by first giving themselves to the Lord. Note, [1.] We should give ourselves to God; we cannot bestow ourselves better. [2.] When we give ourselves to the Lord, we then give him all we have, to be called for and disposed of according to his will. [3.] Whatever we use or lay out for God, it is only giving to him what is his own. [4.] What we give or bestow for charitable uses will not be accepted of God, nor turn to our advantage, unless we first give ourselves to the Lord. <div eID="gen31549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31550" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle tells them that Titus was desired to go and make a collection among them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">v. 6</reference>), and Titus, he knew, would be an acceptable person to them. He had met with a kind reception among them formerly. They had shown good affection to him, and he had a great love for them. Besides, Titus had already begun this work among them, therefore he was desired to finish it. So that he was, on all accounts, a proper person to be employed; and, when so good a work had already prospered in so good a hand, it would be a pity if it should not proceed and be finished. Note, It is an instance of wisdom to use proper instruments in a work we desire to do well; and the work of charity will often succeed the best when the most proper persons are employed to solicit contributions and dispose of them.
entries.825aad9cbf3025d1bbe0acce86d10cd760b4bbff: <div eID="gen31550" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Charity Urged. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore, as ye abound in every <hi type="italic">thing, in</hi> faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> all diligence, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> your love to us, <hi type="italic">see</hi> that ye abound in this grace also. <hi type="super">8</hi> I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love. <hi type="super">9</hi> For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. <hi type="super">10</hi> And herein I give <hi type="italic">my</hi> advice: for this is expedient for you, who have begun before, not only to do, but also to be forward a year ago. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now therefore perform the doing <hi type="italic">of it;</hi> that as <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a readiness to will, so <hi type="italic">there may be</hi> a performance also out of that which ye have. <hi type="super">12</hi> For if there be first a willing mind, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> accepted according to that a man hath, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not according to that he hath not. <hi type="super">13</hi> For <hi type="italic">I mean</hi> not that other men be eased, and ye burdened: 14 But by an equality, <hi type="italic">that</hi> now at this time your abundance <hi type="italic">may be a supply</hi> for their want, that their abundance also may be <hi type="italic">a supply</hi> for your want: that there may be equality: <hi type="super">15</hi> As it is written, He that <hi type="italic">had gathered</hi> much had nothing over; and he that <hi type="italic">had gathered</hi> little had no lack. <div eID="gen31551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31552" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle uses several cogent arguments to stir up the Corinthians to this good work of charity. <div eID="gen31552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31553" type="x-p"/> I. He urges upon them the consideration of their eminence in other gifts and graces, and would have them excel in this of charity also, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.7">v. 7</reference>. Great address and much holy art are here used by the apostle. When he would persuade the Corinthians to this good thing, he commends them for other good things that were found in them. Most people love to be complimented, especially when we ask a gift of them for ourselves or others; and it is a justice we owe to those in whom God's grace shines to give them their due commendation. Observe here, What it was that the Corinthians abounded in. Faith is mentioned first, for that is the root; and, as <hi type="italic">without faith it is impossible to please God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>), so those who abound in faith will abound in other graces and good works also; and this will work and show itself by love. To their faith was added utterance, which is an excellent gift, and redounds much to the glory of God and the good of the church. Many have faith who want utterance. But these Corinthians excelled most churches in spiritual gifts, and particularly in utterance; and yet this was not in them, as in too many, both the effect and evidence of ignorance; for with their utterance there appeared knowledge, abundance of knowledge. They had a treasury of things new and old, and in their utterance they brought out of this treasury. They abounded also in all diligence. Those who have great knowledge and ready utterance are not always the most diligent Christians. Great talkers are not always the best doers; but these Corinthians were diligent to do, as well as know and talk, well. And further, they had abundant love to their minister; and were not like too many, who, having gifts of their own, are but too apt to slight their ministers, and neglect them. Now to all these good things the apostle desires them to add this grace also, to abound in charity to the poor; that, where so much good was found, there should be found yet more good. Before the apostle proceeds to another argument he takes care to prevent any misapprehensions of his design to impose on them, or to bind heavy burdens upon them by his authority; and tells them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.8">v. 8</reference>) he does not speak by commandment, or in a way of authority. I give <hi type="italic">my advice,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10">v. 10</reference>. He took occasion from the forwardness of others to propose what would be expedient for them, and would prove the sincerity of their love, or be the genuine effect and evidence thereof. Note, A great difference should be made between plain and positive duty, and the improvement of a present opportunity of doing or getting good. Many a thing which is good for us to do, yet can not be said to be, by express and indispensable commandment, our duty at this or that time. <div eID="gen31553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31554" type="x-p"/> II. Another argument is taken from the consideration of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. The best arguments for Christian duties are those that are taken from the love of Christ, <hi type="italic">that constraineth us.</hi> The example of the churches of Macedonia was such as the Corinthians should imitate; but the example of our Lord Jesus Christ should have much greater influence. And <hi type="italic">you know,</hi> saith the apostle, <hi type="italic">the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">that though he was rich,</hi> as being God, equal in power and glory with the Father, rich in all the glory and blessedness of the upper world, <hi type="italic">yet for your sakes he became poor;</hi> not only did become man for us, but he became poor also. He was born in poor circumstances, lived a poor life, and died in poverty; and this was for our sakes, that we thereby might be made rich, rich in the love and favour of God, rich in the blessings and promises of the new covenant, rich in the hopes of eternal life, being heirs of the kingdom. This is a good reason why we should be charitable to the poor out of what we have, because we ourselves live upon the charity of the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen31554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31555" type="x-p"/> III. Another argument is taken from their good purposes, and their forwardness to begin this good work. As to this he tells them, 1. It was expedient for them to perform what they purposed, and finish what they had begun, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10-2Cor.8.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. What else did their good purposes and good beginnings signify? Good purposes, indeed, are good things; they are like buds and blossoms, pleasant to behold, and give hopes of good fruit; but they are lost, and signify nothing, without performances. So good beginnings are amiable; but we shall lose the benefit unless there be perseverance, and we bring forth fruit to perfection. Seeing therefore the Corinthians had shown a readiness to will, he would have them be careful also in the performance, according to their ability. For, 2. This would be acceptable to God. <hi type="italic">This willing mind is accepted</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.12">v. 12</reference>), when accompanied with sincere endeavours. When men purpose that which is good, and endeavour, according to their ability, to perform also, God will accept of what they have, or can do, and not reject them for what they have not, and what is not in their power to do: and this is true as to other things besides the work of charity. But let us note here that this scripture will by no means justify those who think good meanings are enough, or that good purposes, and the profession of a willing mind, are sufficient to save them. It is accepted, indeed, where there is a performance as far as we are able, and when Providence hinders the performance, as in David's case concerning building a house for the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.1-2Sam.7.29">2 Sam. vii</reference>. <div eID="gen31555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31556" type="x-p"/> IV. Another argument is taken from the discrimination which the divine Providence makes in the distribution of the things of this world, and the mutability of human affairs, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.13-2Cor.8.15">v. 13-15</reference>. The force of the arguing seems to be this:—Providence gives to some more of the good things of this world, and to some less, and that with this design, that those who have a greater <hi type="italic">abundance may supply those who are in want,</hi> that there may be room for charity. And further, considering the mutability of human affairs, and how soon there may be an alteration, so that those who now have an abundance may stand in need of being supplied themselves in their wants, this should induce them to be charitable while they are able. It is the will of God that, by our mutually supplying one another, there should <hi type="italic">be some sort of equality;</hi> not an <hi type="italic">absolute</hi> equality indeed, or such a levelling as would destroy property, for in such a case there could be no exercise of charity. But as in works of charity there should be an equitable proportion observed, that the burden should not lie too heavy on some, while others are wholly eased, so all should think themselves concerned to supply those who are in want. This is illustrated by the instance of gathering and distributing manna in the wilderness, concerning which (as we may read, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.1-Exod.16.36">Exod. xvi.</reference>) it was the duty of every family, and all in the family, to gather what they could, which, when it was gathered, was put into some common receptacle for each family, whence the master of the family distributed to every one as he had occasion, to some more than they were able, through age and infirmity, to gather up; to others less than they gathered, because they did not need so much: and thus <hi type="italic">he that had gathered much</hi> (more than he had occasion for) had nothing over, when a communication was made to him <hi type="italic">that had gathered little,</hi> who by this method had no lack. Note, Such is the condition of men in this world that we mutually depend on one another, and should help one another. Those who have ever so much of this world have no more than food and raiment; and those who have but a little of this world seldom want these; nor, indeed, should those who have abundance suffer others to want, but be ready to afford supply.
entries.b488e5bb7f889f2e9ad147cf44eb7350b599910f: <div eID="gen31556" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Commendations of Titus and Others. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> But thanks <hi type="italic">be</hi> to God, which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus for you. <hi type="super">17</hi> For indeed he accepted the exhortation; but being more forward, of his own accord he went unto you. <hi type="super">18</hi> And we have sent with him the brother, whose praise <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the gospel throughout all the churches; <hi type="super">19</hi> And not <hi type="italic">that</hi> only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and <hi type="italic">declaration of</hi> your ready mind: <hi type="super">20</hi> Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: <hi type="super">21</hi> Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. <hi type="super">22</hi> And we have sent with them our brother, whom we have oftentimes proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent, upon the great confidence which <hi type="italic">I have</hi> in you. <hi type="super">23</hi> Whether <hi type="italic">any do enquire</hi> of Titus, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> my partner and fellowhelper concerning you: or our brethren <hi type="italic">be enquired of, they are</hi> the messengers of the churches, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the glory of Christ. <hi type="super">24</hi> Wherefore show ye to them, and before the churches, the proof of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf. <div eID="gen31557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31558" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle commends the brethren who were sent to them to collect their charity; and as it were, gives them letters credential, that, if they <hi type="italic">were enquired after</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">v. 23</reference>), if any should be inquisitive or suspicious concerning them, it might be known who they were and how safely they might be trusted. <div eID="gen31558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31559" type="x-p"/> I. He commends Titus, 1. For his earnest care and great concern of heart for them, and desire in all things to promote their welfare. This is mentioned with thankfulness to God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16">v. 16</reference>), and it is cause of thankfulness if God hath put it into the hearts of any to do us or others any good. 2. For his readiness to this present service. He accepted the office, and was forward to go upon this good errand, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.17">v. 17</reference>. Asking charity for the relief of others is by many looked upon as a thankless office; yet it is a good office, and what we should not be shy of when we are called to it. <div eID="gen31559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31560" type="x-p"/> II. He commends another brother, who was sent with Titus. It is generally thought that this was Luke. He is commended, 1. As a man whose <hi type="italic">praise was in the gospel through all the churches,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.18">v. 18</reference>. His ministerial services of several kinds were well known, and he had approved himself praiseworthy in what he had done. 2. As one chosen of the churches (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19">v. 19</reference>) and joined with the apostle in his ministration. This was done, it is most likely, at the motion and request of Paul himself; for this reason, <hi type="italic">that no man might blame him in that abundance which was administered by him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.20">v. 20</reference>), so cautious was the apostle to avoid all occasions that evil-minded men might lay hold on to blacken him. He would not give occasion to any to accuse him of injustice or partiality in this affair, and thought it to be his duty, as it is the duty of all Christians, <hi type="italic">to provide for things honest, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men;</hi> that is, to act so prudently as to prevent, as far as we can, all unjust suspicions concerning us, and all occasions of scandalous imputations. Note, We live in a censorious world, and should cut off occasion from those who seek occasion to speak reproachfully. It is the crime of others if they reproach or censure us without occasion; and it is our imprudence at least if we give them any occasion, when there may not be a just cause for them so to do. <div eID="gen31560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31561" type="x-p"/> III. He commends also another brother who was joined with the two former in this affair. This brother is thought to be Apollos. Whoever he was, he had <hi type="italic">approved himself diligent in many things;</hi> and therefore was fit to be employed in this affair. Moreover, he had great desire to this work, because of the confidence or good opinion he had of the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.22">v. 22</reference>), and it is a great comfort to see those employed in good works who have formerly approved themselves diligent. <div eID="gen31561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31562" type="x-p"/> IV. He concludes this point with a general good character of them all (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">v. 23</reference>), as <hi type="italic">fellow-labourers with him</hi> for their welfare; as the <hi type="italic">messengers of the churches;</hi> as the <hi type="italic">glory of Christ,</hi> who were to him for a name and a praise, who brought glory to Christ as instruments and had obtained honour from Christ to be counted faithful and employed in his service. Wherefore, upon the whole, he exhorts them to show their liberality, answerable to the great expectation others had concerning them at this time, that these messengers of the churches, and the churches themselves, might see a full <hi type="italic">proof of their love</hi> to God and to their afflicted brethren, and that it was with good reason the apostle had even <hi type="italic">boasted on their behalf,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.24">v. 24</reference>. Note, The good opinion others entertain of us should be an argument with us to do well.  <chapter eID="2Cor.8"/> <div eID="gen31562" type="x-p"/>

entries.22c67ec17b977ba23b152a4a23bc9a1da7c08a69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17300"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen34472" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1-2Cor.8.24">2Co 8:1-24</reference>. The Collection for the Saints; the Readiness of the Macedonians a Pattern to the Corinthians; Christ the Highest Pattern; Each Is to Give Willingly after His Ability; Titus and Two Others Are the Agents Accredited to Complete the Collection.<div eID="gen34472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17300"/><hi type="bold">1. we do you to wit--</hi>we make known to you.<div eID="gen34473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia--</hi>Their liberality was not of themselves naturally, but of God's grace bestowed on them, and enabling them to be the instrument of God's "grace" to others (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19">19</reference>). The importance given in this Epistle to the collection, arose as well from Paul's engagement (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.10">Ga 2:10</reference>), as also chiefly from his hope to conciliate the Judaizing Christians at Jerusalem to himself and the Gentile believers, by such an act of love on the part of the latter towards their Jewish brethren. <div eID="gen34474" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4668c14159b9dbd51c64cb8feb705377c5b844e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17301"/><div sID="gen34475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17301"/><hi type="bold">2. trial of affliction--</hi>The Greek expresses, "in affliction (or, 'tribulation') which tested them"; literally, "in a great testing of affliction."<div eID="gen34475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance of their joy--</hi>The greater was the depth of their poverty, the greater was the abundance of their joy. A delightful contrast in terms, and triumph, in fact, of spirit over flesh.<div eID="gen34476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their deep poverty--</hi>Greek, "their poverty down to the death of it."<div eID="gen34477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abounded unto the riches of their liberality--</hi>another beautiful contrast in terms: their poverty had the effect, not of producing stinted gifts, but of "abounding in the riches of liberality" (not as Margin, "simplicity"; though the idea of singleness of motive to God's glory and man's good, probably enters into the idea); (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">Ro 12:8</reference>, and Margin; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.11">2Co 9:11</reference>, Margin; see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.13">2Co 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">Jas 1:5</reference>). <div eID="gen34478" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd27a8a7090a4e6e8ad530d2669ece65dc98e9db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17302"/><div sID="gen34479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17302"/><hi type="bold">3-5. they were willing--</hi>rather, supply from <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.5">2Co 8:5</reference>, the ellipsis thus, "According to their power ... yea, and beyond their power, THEY GAVE."<div eID="gen34479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of themselves--</hi>not only not being besought, but themselves beseeching us. <div eID="gen34480" type="x-p"/>
entries.94d9a5b4077f50edd787d03cbc9568d6d3afef8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17305"/><div sID="gen34484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17305"/><hi type="bold">6. Insomuch that--</hi>As we saw the Macedonians' alacrity in giving, we could not but exhort Titus, that as we collected in Macedonia, so he in Corinth should complete the work of collecting which he had already begun there, lest ye, the wealthy people of Corinth, should be outdone in liberality by the poor Macedonians.<div eID="gen34484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as he had begun--</hi>Greek, "previously begun," namely, the collection at Corinth, before the Macedonians began to contribute, during the visit to Corinth from which he had just returned.<div eID="gen34485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">finish in you the same grace--</hi>complete among you this act of grace or beneficence on your part.<div eID="gen34486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>as well as other things which he had to do among them [Alford]. <div eID="gen34487" type="x-p"/>
entries.760b02381aebcf352a39d02bda24e3e529929504: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17306"/><div sID="gen34488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17306"/><hi type="bold">7. in faith--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.24">2Co 1:24</reference>).<div eID="gen34488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">utterance--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">1Co 1:5</reference>). Not as Alford, "doctrine" or "word."<div eID="gen34489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.1">1Co 8:1</reference>).<div eID="gen34490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diligence--</hi>in everything that is good.<div eID="gen34491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your love to us--</hi>literally, "love from you (that is, on your part) in us" (that is, which has us for its object; which is felt in the case of us). <div eID="gen34492" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6d9c0c5e6c991c508336bc996545de81104e09b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17307"/><div sID="gen34493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17307"/><hi type="bold">8. not by commandment--</hi>"not by way of commandment."<div eID="gen34493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and &c.--</hi>rather, "But by (mention of) the forwardness of others (as an inducement to you), and to prove (literally, 'proving') the sincerity of your love." The Greek is "by means of," not "on account of the forwardness," &c. Bengel, Ellicott, and others translate, "By means of the forwardness of others, proving the sincerity of your love ALSO." The former is the simpler construction in the Greek. <div eID="gen34494" type="x-p"/>
entries.e608aa1aa1a515ea253fe496924d6c550b029e0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17308"/><div sID="gen34495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17308"/><hi type="bold">9. ye know the grace--</hi>the act of gratuitous love whereby the Lord emptied Himself of His previous heavenly glory (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.6">Php 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>) for your sakes.<div eID="gen34495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">became poor--</hi>Yet this is not demanded of you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.14">2Co 8:14</reference>); but merely that, without impoverishing yourselves, you should relieve others with your abundance. If the Lord did so much more, and at so much heavier a cost, for your sakes; much more may you do an act of love to your brethren at so little a sacrifice of self.<div eID="gen34496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be rich--</hi>in the heavenly glory which constitutes His riches, and all other things, so far as is really good for us (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen34497" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed4d8501e7208a939e401f8b921b208acfe5d03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17309"/><div sID="gen34498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17309"/><hi type="bold">10. advice--</hi>Herein he does not (as some misinterpret the passage) disclaim inspiration for the advice he gives; but under the Spirit, states that it is his "opinion" [Alford] or "judgment" [Ellicott, and others], not a command, that so their offering might be free and spontaneous.<div eID="gen34498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>my giving you an advice, not a command.<div eID="gen34499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who have begun before--</hi>"seeing that ye have begun before" the Macedonian churches; "a year ago" should be connected with this clause.<div eID="gen34500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not only to do, but also to be forward--</hi>There were three steps: (1) the forwardness, more literally, "the will"; (2) the setting about it, literally, "doing it"; (3) completion of it [Alford]. In the two former, not only the act, but the intention, the Corinthians preceded the Macedonians. Bengel explains, "Not only to do" FOR THE PAST YEAR, "but also to be forward" or willing FOR THIS YEAR. Ellicott translates, "already," instead of "before": "Ye began already a year ago, not only to do, but also to be forward." It appears hence, that something had been done in the matter a year before; other texts, however, show the collection was not yet paid (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.5">2Co 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">7</reference>). This agrees with one, and only one supposition, namely, that every man had laid by in store the fund from which he was afterwards to contribute, the very case which is shown by <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1Co 16:2</reference> to have existed [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. <div eID="gen34501" type="x-p"/>
entries.ece7058ae10f5c4454fafab55aebe950a560a0c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17310"/><div sID="gen34502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17310"/><hi type="bold">11. perform--</hi>"complete the doing also" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10">2Co 8:10</reference>).<div eID="gen34502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a readiness to will--</hi>Greek, "the readiness of will"; referring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10">2Co 8:10</reference>, where the Greek for "to be forward," ought to be translated as here, "to will."<div eID="gen34503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">performance--</hi>"completion" [Alford], The godly should show the same zeal to finish, as well as to begin well, which the worldly exhibit in their undertakings (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.25">Jr 44:25</reference>). <div eID="gen34504" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0a12b887e0b1d809a3855b578ffe80f4d5f8c74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17311"/><div sID="gen34505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17311"/><hi type="bold">12. For--</hi>Following up the rule "out of that which ye have" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference>), and no more.<div eID="gen34505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a willing mind--</hi>rather, as Greek, "the readiness," namely, to will, referring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference>.<div eID="gen34506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accepted--</hi>Greek "favorably accepted."<div eID="gen34507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to that a man hath--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "a man." Translate, "According to whatsoever it have"; the willing mind, or "readiness" to will, is personified [Alford]. Or better, as Bengel, "He is accepted according to whatsoever he have"; so <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2Co 9:7</reference>, The Lord loveth a cheerful giver." Compare as to David, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.18">1Ki 8:18</reference>. God accepts the will for the deed. He judges not according to what a man has the opportunity to do, but according to what he would do if he had the opportunity (compare <reference osisRef="Mark.14.8">Mr 14:8</reference>; and the widow's mite, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.3">Lu 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen34508" type="x-p"/>
entries.e81296022eca0c9f0b822ef3ac03776eea51259b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17312"/><div sID="gen34509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17312"/><hi type="bold">13. For--</hi>Supply from <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.8">2Co 8:8</reference>, "I speak." My aim is not that others (namely, the saints at Jerusalem) may be relieved at the cost of your being "distressed" (so the Greek for "burdened"). The golden rule is, "Love thy neighbour as thyself," not more than thyself. <div eID="gen34509" type="x-p"/>
entries.b02400ad8dace76a3953e971b8ac4dc3160b8032: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17313"/><div sID="gen34510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17313"/><hi type="bold">14. by an equality--</hi>"by the rule of equality" [Alford]: literally, "Out of equality."<div eID="gen34510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now at this time--</hi>Greek, "at the present juncture" or season.<div eID="gen34511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that their abundance also--</hi>The Greek being distinct from the previous "that," translate, "in order that," namely, at another season, when your relative circumstances may be reversed. The reference is solely to temporal wants and supplies. Those, as Bengel, who quote <reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Ro 15:27</reference> for interpreting it of spiritual supplies from the Jews to the Gentiles, forget that <reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Ro 15:27</reference> refers to the past benefit spiritually, which the Jews have conferred on the Gentiles, as a motive to gratitude on the part of the latter, not to a prospective benefit to be looked for from the former, which the text refers to. <div eID="gen34512" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7ed82fc559de0821361938054c392f73e11df25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17314"/><div sID="gen34513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17314"/>15. (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.18">Ex 16:18</reference>; Septuagint). As God gave an equal portion of manna to all the Israelites, whether they could gather much or little; so Christians should promote by liberality an equality, so that none should need the necessaries of life while others have superfluities. "Our luxuries should yield to our neighbor's comforts; and our comforts to his necessities" [J. Howard]. <div eID="gen34513" type="x-p"/>
entries.de4fd87c32533dc95b973213364f3063f082d97d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17315"/><div sID="gen34514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17315"/>16-17. Returning to the subject of <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>.<div eID="gen34514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>Translate, "Which put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus," as was in myself. My care for you led me to "desire" him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.17">17</reference>, "exhortation," the same Greek); but Titus had of himself the same care, whence he "accepted (gladly) my exhortation" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.17">2Co 8:17</reference>) to go to you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>). <div eID="gen34515" type="x-p"/>
entries.acd1db1b4c4d84ca4ffa2019ed299b1b58ee94ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17317"/><div sID="gen34518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17317"/><hi type="bold">18. the brother, whose praise is in the gospel--</hi>whose praise is known in connection with the Gospel: Luke may be meant; not that "the Gospel" here refers to his written Gospel; but the language implies some one well known throughout the churches, and at that time with Paul, as Luke then was (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">Ac 20:6</reference>). Not a Macedonian, as appears from <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Co 9:4</reference>. Of all Paul's "companions in travel" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19">2Co 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>), Luke was the most prominent, having been his companion in preaching the Gospel at his first entrance into Europe (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">Ac 16:10</reference>). The fact that the person here referred to was "chosen of the churches" as their trustee to travel with Paul in conveying the contribution to Jerusalem, implies that he had resided among them some time before: this is true of Luke, who after parting from Paul at Philippi (as he marks by the change from "we" to "they," <reference osisRef="Acts.16.11">Ac 16:11</reference>) six years before, is now again found in his company in Macedonia. In the interim he had probably become so well known that "his praise was throughout all the churches." Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">2Co 12:18</reference>; Phm 24. He who is faithful in the Gospel will be faithful also in matters of inferior importance [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34518" type="x-p"/>
entries.26d85762815dfe0bf2df701a9602c6a667fd6f9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17318"/><div sID="gen34519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17318"/><hi type="bold">19. not that only--</hi>not only praised in all the churches.<div eID="gen34519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen--</hi>by vote: so the Greek.<div eID="gen34520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the churches--</hi>therefore these companions of Paul are called "messengers of the churches" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2Co 8:23</reference>).<div eID="gen34521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to travel--</hi>to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen34522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with this grace--</hi>Greek, "in the case of this grace," or "gift."<div eID="gen34523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the glory of the same Lord--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "same."<div eID="gen34524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declaration of your ready mind--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "our," not your. This and the previous clause, "to the glory of the same Lord," do not follow "administered by us," but "chosen of the churches to travel," &c. The union of the brother with Paul in this affair of the collection was done to guard against suspicions injurious "to the glory" of the Lord. It was also done in order to produce a "readiness" on the part of Paul and the brother to undertake the office which each, by himself, would have been less ready to undertake, for fear of suspicions arising (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.20">2Co 8:20</reference>) as to their appropriation of any of the money. <div eID="gen34525" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c3a598edb4ab36b6309a78a6ceadf9f9ccacf8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17319"/><div sID="gen34526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17319"/><hi type="bold">20. Avoiding--</hi>taking precautions against this.<div eID="gen34526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in this abundance--</hi>in the case of this abundance. <div eID="gen34527" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5de68ec50374551d211f413a25de4ef7fa48a8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17320"/><div sID="gen34528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17320"/>21. The Septuagint (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pr 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.17">Ro 12:17</reference>). The oldest manuscripts read, "For we provide."<div eID="gen34528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honest things--</hi>"things honorable." <div eID="gen34529" type="x-p"/>
entries.eef6ecad961a67ddd0b3ae095c2fe265229799b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17321"/><div sID="gen34530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17321"/>22. This second brother, Birks supposes to be Trophimus: for a Macedonian is not meant (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Co 9:4</reference>) probably the same as was sent before with Titus (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">2Co 12:18</reference>); and therefore sent from Ephesus, and probably an Ephesian: all this is true of Trophimus.<div eID="gen34530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oftentimes ... in many things--</hi>Join and translate as in the Greek, "many times in many things."<div eID="gen34531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the great confidence which I have in you--</hi>"through the great confidence WHICH HE HAS towards you" [Alford]. Bengel better supports English Version, "We have sent ... through the confidence WHICH WE FEEL in regard to your liberality." <div eID="gen34532" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fa6f4904504e41bf6fab51d1e32b99620531327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17322"/><div sID="gen34533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17322"/><hi type="bold">23. fellow helper concerning you--</hi>Greek, "fellow worker towards you."<div eID="gen34533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our brethren--</hi>the two mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.18">2Co 8:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.22">22</reference>.<div eID="gen34534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">messengers--</hi>rather, as the Greek, "apostles": in the less strict sense (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.14">Ac 14:14</reference>).<div eID="gen34535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the churches--</hi>sent by the churches, as we are by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.25">Php 2:25</reference>). There was in the synagogue an ecclesiastical officer, called "the angel of the Church," whence the title seems derived (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1">Re 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen34536" type="x-p"/>
entries.4be30871fa500fb038a1b46756efc196490b067f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17323"/><div sID="gen34537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17323"/>24. The oldest manuscripts read "[continue] manifesting to them in the face of the churches the manifestation of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf." <chapter eID="2Cor.8"/>

entries.5a8afec52b759fb29e1fb0b0ab2d67b9ef9b0b76: <div eID="gen49193" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen49194" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49195" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49195" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49194" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49196" type="x-p"/> The apostle stirs them up to make a collection for the poor Christians at Jerusalem, by the very liberal contributions of the people of Macedonia for the same purpose, who were comparatively a poor people, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1-2Cor.8.5">2Cor 8:1-5</reference>. He tells them that he had desired Titus to finish this good work among them which he had begun; hoping that as they abounded in many excellent gifts and graces, they would abound in this also, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6-2Cor.8.8">2Cor 8:6-8</reference>. He exhorts them to this by the example of Jesus Christ, who, though rich, subjected himself to voluntary poverty, that they might be enriched, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Cor 8:9</reference>. He shows them that this contribution, which had been long ago begun, should have been long since finished, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10">2Cor 8:10</reference>. And that they should do every thing with a ready and willing mind, according to the ability which God had given them; that abundance should not prevail on one hand, while pinching poverty ruled on the other; but that there should be an equality, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11-2Cor.8.14">2Cor 8:11-14</reference>. He shows from the distribution of the manna in the wilderness, that the design of God was, that every member of his spiritual household should have the necessaries of life, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.15">2Cor 8:15</reference>. He tells them that he had now sent Titus, and another with him, to Corinth, to complete this great work, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16-2Cor.8.22">2Cor 8:16-22</reference>. The character which he gives of Titus and the others employed in this business, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2Cor 8:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.24">2Cor 8:24</reference>. <div eID="gen49196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49197" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen49197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49198" type="x-p"/> Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit - In all our dignified version very few ill-constructed sentences can be found; however here is one, and the worst in the book. We do you to wit is in the original γνωριζομεν δε ὑμιν, we make known unto you. This is plain and intelligible, the other is not so; and the form is now obsolete. <div eID="gen49198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49199" type="x-p"/> The grace of God bestowed - Dr. Whitby has made it fully evident that the χαρις Θεου signifies the charitable contribution made by the Churches in Macedonia, to which they were excited by the grace or influence of God upon their hearts; and that δεδομενην εν cannot signify bestowed on, but given in. That χαρις means liberality, appears from <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Cor 8:6</reference> : We desired Titus that as he had begun, so he would finish την χαριν ταυτην, this charitable contribution. And <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.7">2Cor 8:7</reference> : That ye abound εν ταυτῃ τῃ χαριτι, in this liberal contribution. And <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19">2Cor 8:19</reference> : Who was chosen of the Church to travel with us συν τῃ χαριτι ταυτῃ, with this charitable contribution, which is administered - which is to be dispensed, by us. So <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.8">2Cor 9:8</reference> : God is able to make πασαν χαριν, all liberality, to abound towards you. And <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.3">1Cor 16:3</reference> : To bring την χαριν, your liberality, to the poor saints. Hence χαρις, is by Hesychius and Phavorinus interpreted a gift, as it is here by the apostle: Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.15">2Cor 9:15</reference>. This charity is styled the grace of God, either from its exceeding greatness, (as the cedars of God and mountains of God signify great cedars and great mountains, <reference osisRef="Psa.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.80.10">Psa 80:10</reference>); or rather, it is called so as proceeding from God, who is the dispenser of all good, and the giver of this disposition; for the motive of charity must come from him. So, in other places, the zeal of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Rom 10:2</reference>; the love of God, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">2Cor 5:14</reference>; the grace of God, <reference osisRef="Tit.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>. <div eID="gen49199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49200" type="x-p"/> The Churches of Macedonia - These were Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, etc.
entries.96ae678588325dd94a6056442194c36514294323: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen49200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49201" type="x-p"/> In a great trial of affliction - The sense of this verse is the following: The Macedonians, though both poor and persecuted, rejoiced exceedingly that an opportunity was afforded them of doing good to their more impoverished and more persecuted brethren. We can scarcely ever speak of poverty and affliction in an absolute sense; they are only comparative. Even the poor are called to relieve those who are poorer than themselves; and the afflicted, to comfort those who are more afflicted than they are. The poor and afflicted Churches of Macedonia felt this duty, and therefore came forward to the uttermost of their power to relieve their more impoverished and afflicted brethren in Judea.
entries.c858c4c305e4da02847988bc2cdfca4ddf8a4943: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen49201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49202" type="x-p"/> For to their power, etc. - In their liberality they had no rule but their ability; they believed they were bound to contribute all they could; and even this rule they transgressed, for they went beyond their power - they deprived themselves for a time of the necessaries of life, in order to give to others who were destitute even of necessaries.
entries.630a9f41a912529b0568b816f35cd578bb23c68e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen49202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49203" type="x-p"/> Praying us with much entreaty - We had not to solicit them to this great act of kindness; they even entreated us to accept their bounty, and to take on ourselves the administration or application of it to the wants of the poor in Judea.
entries.9c9ba60519c3171935e0dd454701e70410c67efd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen49203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49204" type="x-p"/> Not as we hoped - They far exceeded our expectations, for they consecrated themselves entirely to the work of God; giving themselves and all they possessed first unto the Lord; and then, as they saw that it was the will of God that they should come especially forward in this charitable work, they gave themselves to us, to assist to the uttermost in providing relief for the suffering Christians in Judea.
entries.f79591f5eafa784c63d49113e5209a4245569166: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen49204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49205" type="x-p"/> That we desired Titus - Titus had probably laid the plan of this contribution when he was before at Corinth, according to the direction given by the apostle, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.1">1Cor 16:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen49205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49206" type="x-p"/> The same grace - Liberality. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">2Cor 8:1</reference>.
entries.b71458b2bada734b9189b78f368de95272b0ef15: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen49206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49207" type="x-p"/> As ye abound in every thing - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">1Cor 1:5</reference>. In faith, crediting the whole testimony of God; in utterance, λογῳ, in doctrine, knowing what to teach: knowledge of God's will, and prudence to direct you in teaching and doing it; in diligence, to amend all that is wrong among you, and to do what is right; and in love to us, whom now ye prize as the apostles of the Lord, and your pastors in him. <div eID="gen49207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49208" type="x-p"/> Abound in this grace also - Be as eminent for your charitable disposition as ye are for your faith, doctrine, knowledge, diligence, and love.
entries.057e8b9c0113f304a85ac31126c923295c347abe: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen49208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49209" type="x-p"/> I speak not by commandment - I do not positively order this; I assume no right or authority over your property; what you devote of your substance to charitable purposes must be your own work, and a free-will offering. <div eID="gen49209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49210" type="x-p"/> The forwardness of others - Viz. the Churches of Macedonia, which had already exerted themselves so very much in this good work. And the apostle here intimates that he takes this opportunity to apprise them of the zeal of the Macedonians, lest those at Corinth, who excelled in every other gift, should be outdone in this. Their own honor, if better motives were absent, would induce them to exert themselves, that they might not be outdone by others. And then, as they had professed great love for the apostle, and this was a service that lay near his heart, they would prove the sincerity of that professed love by a liberal contribution for the afflicted and destitute Jewish Christians.
entries.1ed9a7424775f8d6bc855d2c3e6775b924bd8ca6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen49210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49211" type="x-p"/> For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ - This was the strongest argument of all; and it is urged home by the apostle with admirable address. <div eID="gen49211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49212" type="x-p"/> Ye know - Ye are acquainted with God's ineffable love in sending Jesus Christ into the world; and ye know the grace - the infinite benevolence of Christ himself. <div eID="gen49212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49213" type="x-p"/> That, though he was rich - The possessor, as he was the creator, of the heavens and the earth; for your sakes he became poor - he emptied himself, and made himself of no reputation, and took upon himself the form of a servant, and humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross; that ye, through his poverty - through his humiliation and death, might be rich - might regain your forfeited inheritance, and be enriched with every grace of his Holy Spirit, and brought at last to his eternal glory. <div eID="gen49213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49214" type="x-p"/> If Jesus Christ, as some contend, were only a mere man, in what sense could he be said to be rich? His family was poor in Bethlehem; his parents were very poor also; he himself never possessed any property among men from the stable to the cross; nor had he any thing to bequeath at his death but his peace. And in what way could the poverty of one man make a multitude rich? These are questions which, on the Socinian scheme, can never be satisfactorily answered.
entries.ba45bd86fa097b88e206831d7d3183b8cdb674f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen49214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49215" type="x-p"/> Herein I give my advice - For I speak not by way of commandment, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.8">2Cor 8:8</reference>. <div eID="gen49215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49216" type="x-p"/> For this is expedient for you - It is necessary you should do this to preserve a consistency of conduct; for ye began this work a year ago, and it is necessary that ye should complete it as soon as possible. <div eID="gen49216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49217" type="x-p"/> Not only to do, but also to be forward - Το ποιησαι - και το θελειν, literally, to do and to will; but as the will must be before the deed, θελειν, must be taken here in the sense of delight, as it frequently means in the Old and New Testaments. See several examples in Whitby. <div eID="gen49217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49218" type="x-p"/> Some MSS. transpose the words: allowing this, there is no difficulty. <div eID="gen49218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49219" type="x-p"/> A year ago - Απο περυσι. It was about a year before this that the apostle, in his first epistle, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1Cor 16:2</reference>, had exhorted them to make this contribution and there is no doubt that they, in obedience to his directions, had begun to lay up in store for this charitable purpose; he therefore wishes them to complete this good work, and thus show that they were not led to it by the example of the Macedonians, seeing they themselves had been first movers in this business.
entries.1f92702c3fc166371fb7c0c22ebb79a9f02b020d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen49219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49220" type="x-p"/> A readiness to will, so there may be a performance - Ye have willed and purposed this; now perform it. <div eID="gen49220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49221" type="x-p"/> Out of that which ye have - Give as God has enabled you; and give as God has disposed you. He requires each man to do as he can; and accepts the will where the means are wanting to perform the deed.
entries.36cdc11231208a2590dcc3e070e423367419744e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen49221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49222" type="x-p"/> According to that a man hath - According to his real property; not taking that which belongs to his own family, and is indispensably necessary for their support; and not taking that which belongs to others; viz. what he owes to any man.
entries.e1e46bf2f8a8061a0322d89ed880cce42bc17edd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen49222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49223" type="x-p"/> That other men be eased - I do not design that you should impoverish yourselves in order that others may live affluently.
entries.dd60c3aa0d13285d74077e637308195bcc7eaed6: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen49223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49224" type="x-p"/> But by an equality - That you may do to those who are distressed now, as, on a change of circumstances, you would wish them to do to you. And I only wish that of your abundance you would now minister to their wants; and it may be that there abundance may yet supply your wants; for so liable are all human affairs to change, that it is as possible that you rich Corinthians should need the charitable help of others as it is that those Jews, who once had need of nothing, should now be dependent on your bounty. <div eID="gen49224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49225" type="x-p"/> That there may be equality - That ye may exert yourselves so in behalf of those poor people that there may be between you an equality in the necessaries of life; your abundance supplying them with that of which they are utterly destitute.
entries.1eb3edf73bd97e063f174745b83ef96344b37992: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen49225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49226" type="x-p"/> He that had gathered much, had nothing over - On the passage to which the apostle alludes, <reference osisRef="Exo.16.18">Exo 16:18</reference>, I have stated that, probably, every man gathered as much manna as he could, and when he brought it home and measured it by the omer, (for this was the measure for each man's eating), if he had a surplus it went to the supply of some other family that had not been able to collect enough; the family being large, and the time in which the manna might be gathered, before the heat of the day, not being sufficient to collect a supply for so numerous a household; several of whom might be so confined as not to be able to collect for themselves. Thus there was an equality among the Israelites in reference to this thing; and in this light these words of St. Paul lead us to view the passage. To apply this to the present case: the Corinthians, in the course of God's providence, had gathered more than was absolutely necessary for their own support; by giving the surplus to the persecuted and impoverished Christian Jews these would be an equality; both would then possess the necessaries of life, though still the one might have more property than the other.
entries.b7b0a7075a2d33290b49a63829ea60d55c4b163c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen49226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49227" type="x-p"/> But thanks be to God - He thanks God who had already disposed the heart of Titus to attend to this business; and, with his usual address, considers all this as done in the behalf of the Corinthian Church; and that though the poor Christians in Judea are to have the immediate benefit, yet God put honor upon them in making them his instruments in supplying the wants of others. He who is an almoner to God Almighty is highly honored indeed.
entries.f1a5a92d8c2e71f53f79a09fdfc4e2a6d27348c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen49227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49228" type="x-p"/> He accepted the exhortation - I advised him to visit you and excite you to this good work, and I found that he was already disposed in his heart to do it; God put this earnest care in the heart of Titus for you, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16">2Cor 8:16</reference>.
entries.1e2c1252ec15ea63f42a313e6e7e926e7fc4e7b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen49228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49229" type="x-p"/> The brother, whose praise is in the Gospel - Who this brother was we cannot tell; some suppose it was St. Luke, who wrote a gospel, and who was the companion of St. Paul in several of his travels; others think it was Silas; others, Barnabas; others, Mark; and others, Apollos. Neither ancients nor moderns agree in either; but Luke, John, and Mark, seem to have the most probable opinions in their favor. Whoever the person was he was sufficiently known to the Corinthians, as we learn by what the apostle says of him in this place.
entries.75181383ab2370256b917575d49ac36a24b89679: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen49229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49230" type="x-p"/> Chosen of the Churches to travel with us - Χειροτονηθεις· Appointed by a show of hands; from χειρ the hand, and τεινω, to extend. This appointment, by the suffrage of the Churches, seems to refer more to St. Luke than any one else; unless we suppose he refers to the transaction, <reference osisRef="Act.15.40">Act 15:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.15.41">Act 15:41</reference>, and then it would appear that Silas is the person intended. <div eID="gen49230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49231" type="x-p"/> With this grace - Liberal contribution. See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">2Cor 8:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen49231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49232" type="x-p"/> Your ready mind - Your willingness to relieve them. But, instead of ὑμων, your, ἡμων, our, is the reading of almost all the best MSS. and all the versions. This is, doubtless, the reading.
entries.f4554f61d5c384d4c014e49058ce7088a0c8a8ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen49232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49233" type="x-p"/> Avoiding this, that no man should blame us - Taking this prudent caution to have witnesses of our conduct, and such as were chosen by the Churches themselves, that we might not be suspected of having either embezzled or misapplied their bounty, See the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.4">1Cor 16:4</reference>.
entries.706d72f56581e0d62af3b4f84b0861e9756dfc1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen49233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49234" type="x-p"/> Providing for honest things - Taking care to act so as not only to be clear in the sight of God, but also to be clear in the sight of all men; avoiding even the appearance of evil. I wish the reader to refer to the excellent note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.4">1Cor 16:4</reference> (note), which I have extracted from Dr. Paley.
entries.2b6ceabbab679c77e37e5428bbf0967c0cc000f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen49234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49235" type="x-p"/> We have sent with them - Titus and, probably, Luke, our brother, probably Apollos. <div eID="gen49235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49236" type="x-p"/> Now much more diligent - Finding that I have the fullest confidence in your complete reformation and love to me, he engages in this business with alacrity, and exceeds even his former diligence.
entries.0f6945b5156579bd0ff2ab40d87af4ab5045bde1: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen49236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49237" type="x-p"/> Whether any do inquire of Titus - Should it be asked, Who is this Titus? I answer, he is my companion, and my fellow laborer in reference to you; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">2Cor 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">2Cor 7:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.7">2Cor 7:7</reference>. Should any inquire, Who are these brethren, Luke and Apollos? I answer, They are Αποστολοι, apostles of the Churches, and intensely bent on promoting the glory of Christ.
entries.1dc899ab4aaa0eabeb834727e62571f86bf0df63: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen49237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49238" type="x-p"/> Wherefore show ye to them, and before the Churches, etc. - Seeing they are persons every way worthy in themselves, and coming to you on such an important occasion, and so highly recommended, receive them affectionately; and let them thus see that the very high character I have given of you is not exaggerated, and that you are as ready in every work of charity as I have stated you to be. Act in this for your honor. <div eID="gen49238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49239" type="x-p"/> 1. The whole of this chapter and the following is occupied in exciting the richer followers of Christ to be liberal to the poorer; the obligation of each to be so, the reasons on which that obligation is founded, the arguments to enforce the obligation from those reasons, are all clearly stated, and most dexterously and forcibly managed. These two chapters afford a perfect model for a Christian minister who is pleading the cause of the poor. <div eID="gen49239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49240" type="x-p"/> 2. In the management of charities a man ought carefully to avoid the least suspicion of avarice, self-interest, and unfaithfulness. How few persons are entirely free from the upbraidings of their own consciences in the matter of alms! But who will be able to hear the upbraidings of Christ at the time of death and judgment? No man can waste without injustice, or neglect without sin, those things of which he is only the dispenser and steward. <div eID="gen49240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49241" type="x-p"/> 3. God has not settled an equality among men by their birth to the end that this equality might be the work of his grace. He has put the temporal portion of the poor into the hands of the rich, and the spiritual portion of the rich into the hands of the poor, on purpose to keep up a good understanding betwixt the members of the same body by a mutual dependence on one another. He who withholds the part belonging to the poor steals more from himself than from them. Let every one answer this admirable design of God, and labor to re-establish equality: the poor, in praying much for the rich; and the rich, in giving much to the poor. See Quesnel.  <chapter eID="2Cor.8"/> <div eID="gen49241" type="x-p"/>

entries.444cb65e8425b8df3af8d849451a6cb4f2e010df:
Introduction of 2nd Corinthians Chapter 8

IN the previous chapter the apostle had expressed his entire confidence in the ready obedience, of the Corinthians in all things. To this confidence he had been led by the promptitude with which they had complied with his commands in regard to the case of discipline there, and by the respect which they had shown to Titus, whom he had sent to them. All that he had ever said in their favour had been realized; all that had ever been asked of them had been accomplished. The object of his Statement in the close of 2Cor 7 seems to have been to excite them to diligence in completing the collection which they had begun for the poor and afflicted saints of Judea. On the consideration of that subject, which lay so near his heart, he now enters; and this chapter and the following are occupied with suggesting arguments and giving directions for a liberal contribution.

Paul had given directions for taking up this collection in the first epistle. See 2Cor 8:1, seq. Comp. Rom 15:26. This collection he had given Titus direction to take up when he went to Corinth. See 2Cor 8:6-17. But from some cause it had not been completed, 2Cor 8:10,11. What that cause was, is not stated; but it may have been possibly the disturbances which had existed there, or the opposition of the enemies of Paul, or the attention which was necessarily bestowed in regulating the affairs of the church. But in order that the contribution might be made, and might be a liberal one, Paul presses on their attention several considerations designed to excite them to give freely. The chapter is, therefore, of importance to us, as it is a statement of the duty of giving liberally to the cause of benevolence, and of the motives by which it should be done. In the presentation of this subject, Paul urges upon them the following considerations:

He appeals to the very liberal example of the churches of Macedonia, where, though they were exceedingly poor, they had contributed with great cheerfulness and liberality to the object, 2Cor 8:1-5.

From their example he had been induced to desire Titus to lay the subject before the church at Corinth, and to finish the collection which he had begun, 2Cor 8:6.

He directs them to abound in this, not as a matter of commandment, but excited by the example of others, 2Cor 8:7,8.

He appeals to them by the love of the Saviour; reminds them that though he was rich, yet he became poor, and that they were bound to imitate his example, 2Cor 8:9.

He reminds them of their intention to make such a contribution, and of the effort which they had made a year before; and though they had been embarrassed in it, and might find it difficult still to give as much as they had intended, or as much as they would wish, still it would be acceptable to God. For if there was a willing mind, God accepted the offering,2Cor 8:10-12.

He assures them that it was not his wish to burden or oppress them. All that he desired was that there should be an equality in all the churches, 2Cor 8:13-15.

To show them how much he was interested in this, he thanks God that he had put it into the heart of Titus to engage in it. And in order more effectually to secure it, he says that he had sent with Titus a brother who was well known, and whose praise was in all the churches. He had done this in order that the churches might have entire confidence that the contribution would be properly distributed. Paul did not wish it to be intrusted to himself. He would leave no room for suspicion in regard to his own character; he would furnish the utmost security to the churches that their wishes were complied with. He desired to act honestly not only in the sight of the Lord, but to furnish evidence of his entire honesty to men, 2Cor 8:16-21.

To secure the same object he had also sent another brother; and these three brethren he felt willing to recommend as faithful and tried--as men in whom the church at Corinth might repose the utmost confidence, 2Cor 8:22-24.

Verse 1. Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit. We make known to you; we inform you. The phrase, "we do you to Wit," is used in Tindal's translation, and means, "we cause you to know." The purpose for which Paul informed them of the liberality of the churches of Macedonia was to excite them to similar liberality.

Of the grace of God, etc. The favour which God had shown them in exciting a spirit of liberality, and in enabling them to contribute to the fund for supplying the wants of the poor saints at Jerusalem. The word "grace" (χαριν) is sometimes used in the sense of gift, and the phrase "gift of God" some have supposed mast mean very great gift, where the words "of God" may be designed to mark anything very eminent or excellent, as in the phrase "cedars of God," "mountains of God," denoting very great cedars, very great mountains. Some critics (as Macknight, Bloomfield, Locke, and others) have supposed that this means that the churches of Macedonia had been able to contribute largely to the aid of the saints at Judea. But the more obvious and correct interpretation, as I apprehend, is that which is implied in the common version, that the phrase "grace of God" means that God had bestowed on them grace to give according to their ability in this cause. According to this it is implied,

(1.) that a disposition to contribute to the cause of benevolence is to be traced to God. He is its Author. He excites it. It is not a plant of native growth in the human heart; but a large and liberal spirit of benevolence is one of the effects of his grace, and is to be traced to him.

(2.) It is a favour bestowed on a church when God excites in it a spirit of benevolence. It is one of the evidences of his love. And indeed there cannot be a higher proof of the favour of God, than when by his grace he inclines and enables us to contribute largely to meliorate the condition, and to alleviate the wants of our fellow-men. Perhaps the apostle here meant delicately to hint this. He did not therefore say coldly that the churches of Macedonia had contributed to this object, but he speaks of it as a favour shown to them by God that they were able to do it. And he meant, probably, gently to intimate to the Corinthians that it would be an evidence that they were enjoying the favour of God, if they should contribute in like manner.

The churches of Macedonia. Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea. For an account of Macedonia, Acts 16:9; Rom 15:26. Of these churches, that at Philippi seems to have been most distinguished for liberality, (Php 4:10,15,16,18,) though it is probable that other churches contributed according to their ability, as they are commended (comp. 2Cor 9:2) without distinction.

(*) "to wit" "We make known to you" (a) "churches of Macedonia" 2Cor 9:2,4
entries.0b136df9d0d5f15930bd4794c86871427188df8d:
Verse 2. How that, in a great trial of affliction. When it might be supposed they were unable to give; when many would suppose they needed the aid of others; or when it might be supposed their minds would be wholly engrossed with their own concerns. The trial to which the apostle here refers was doubtless some persecution which Was excited against them, probably by the Jews. Acts 16:20, 17:5.

The abundance of their joy. Their joy arising from the hopes and promises of the gospel. Notwithstanding their persecutions, their joy has abounded, and the effect of their joy has been seen in the liberal contribution which they have made. Their joy could not be repressed by their persecution, and they cheerfully contributed largely to the aid of others.

And their deep poverty. Their very low estate of poverty was made to contribute liberally to the wants of others. It is implied here,
